question: The pitch is that specs kept as a pile of markdown files are tiring to work with. Is there anything behind that beyond taste — has the cost to a team ever been measured, and what exactly makes the reviewing hard?
answer: The workflow is fine; the artifact is not. Independent benchmarks measured markdown-spec workflows at roughly an order of magnitude slower than plain AI coding, largely from review burden: a typical pipeline produces five or more files (principles, specification, plan, research, tasks) that share context, repeat each other and ask a reviewer to hold the whole graph in their head. Three criticisms recur — review fatigue (long undifferentiated prose, no progressive disclosure), markdown being a thin format (no diagrams, fragile tables, no interactivity, no semantic anchors beyond headings), and "waterfall in markdown" (gated phases duplicating background because cross-linking is weak). HTML addresses all three in one file and still reads in any browser.
core: An order of magnitude slower than plain AI coding, largely review burden.
note: The spec's own #context, the only place the benchmark figure appears.
visitor: The landing page asserts markdown is tiring to read. A visitor weighing adoption wants to know whether that is an aesthetic preference or a measured cost.

question: There is a command that checks a spec against a grammar and can annotate a pull request. Before that existed, what actually stopped someone committing a malformed spec, and which readers could not tell?
answer: Implicitly, and only for a human with the file open: CSS marked a <spec-delta> with no op= as "MISSING OP", JS logged a console warning when a <spec-out-of-scope> <li> lacked defer-to=, and slash-command prose told the author what was required. A reviewer opening spec.html saw the visible failures; a CI pipeline did not. There was no mechanical gate. Authors, CI bots and editor extensions are the users, and they had nothing — which is why the strategy plan named a validator plus a formal schema as Tier 1's first piece, since every later surface (VS Code diagnostics, MCP-exposed checks, the TypeScript kernel) depends on shared rules.
core: The grammar lived implicitly in CSS, JS warnings and prose; there was no mechanical gate.
visitor: The site advertises `npx @spectastic/cli validate` with SARIF output for CI. A visitor asks what the project did before it had a mechanical gate.

question: Installing this gives one command on my PATH. It did not start that way — there was a Python piece once. What forced the two to become one, and what did the consolidation actually improve?
answer: The Python `scripts/spectastic init` and the Node `spectastic validate` both wanted the same `spectastic` binary name on PATH, and exactly one can own it; spec 002 §6 Assumption #4 had already acknowledged the transition cost and named "retire Python once the Node CLI reaches parity" as the resolution. Porting bought one install story (`npm i -g @spectastic/cli` rather than chmod +x on a downloaded Python file), one binary on PATH (no spectastic-init renaming compromise), and shared lifecycle and test infrastructure across init and validate and future subcommands. The Python script's 1.0 behaviour is the contract.
core: Two CLIs wanted the same binary name on PATH and only one can own it.
visitor: The site's install story is a single CLI. A visitor who finds references to a Python script wants to know what happened to it.

question: Suppose I wanted a colleague to try this before any of it was on a public registry. What would I have had to talk them through, and which later part of the product was held up until that was sorted?
answer: Cloning the repository, running pnpm install and then npm link — Tier 1 had shipped @spectastic/cli and @spectastic/schema as Node packages but neither had been published to npm. The spec is the follow-up that 003 deferred as TBD-npm-publish, and it closes the gap before Tier 3's VS Code extension starts telling users to `npm i`.
core: Cloning plus pnpm-install plus npm link; Tier 3's VS Code extension was waiting.
note: The spec's own #context, a single short section.
visitor: The site tells visitors to run an npx command. A visitor asks what adoption looked like before publishing existed.

question: Six of the commands call a language model to do their work. Putting a real one in a continuous-integration pipeline was looked at and turned down — what went wrong with the cheap option and what went wrong with the good one?
answer: Small models fit but are not reproducible: Gemma 2 2B at q4 sits inside GitHub Actions' 7GB easily, yet intermittently produces malformed JSON, drops closing braces and picks slightly different phrasings even at temperature 0, which turns every failing test into "is this a real regression or just the model being non-deterministic". A hosted model is reproducible enough but burns API spend on every push and leaks the key to forked pull requests. Stub providers with hand-curated responses are deterministic and fast and still catch what integration tests exist for — prompt-format drift, parse-shape breakage and wiring bugs — so the load-bearing piece is the injection point itself.
core: Small models are non-deterministic even at temperature 0; a hosted model costs money per push and leaks the key to forked PRs.
note: The spec's own #context, two parts. The fuller reasoning lives in a project memory outside the corpus, so #context is the only address holding it.
visitor: The site says the commands run inside an AI agent. A visitor who maintains a CI pipeline asks how anything model-backed is tested without being flaky or expensive.

question: Every page here can be flipped from bright to muted. Is a second typeface-and-shape treatment on offer as well, and how do those two controls sit alongside one another?
answer: It was a mode toggle wearing the word theme: a single [data-theme-toggle] button flipping an html.dark class and saving localStorage['spectastic-theme'], which only ever changed colour against one typographic look. Wanting a second visual identity — heavier type, derived from the reference design — without giving up dark mode in either look forces the two concerns apart: a theme is the visual identity (typography and structure: weights, surfaces, radii, rule weights, spacing) and a mode is the colour palette (light or dark). They are orthogonal, so the look-set is a 2x2 matrix rather than a single switch.
core: It was a mode toggle, not a theme toggle; theme and mode are orthogonal, giving a 2x2 matrix.
visitor: Every page on the site is a rendered artifact with a visible light/dark control. A visitor notices it and asks what else is adjustable.

question: Once the last task is ticked and the code is written, is there anything that tells the next person how to run the feature and satisfy themselves it works? What showed that this was a real hole rather than a nice-to-have?
answer: Validation. A good merge request reads what, why, how and validation; spectastic had homes for three of those — tasks, spec and plan — and validation was homeless, so once /implement ticked the last box nothing answered "it's built, how do I run it, see it work, and what do I turn on?". Dogfooding spec-tictactoe proved it real: the UI shipped with no way to tell how to run the whole thing, and getting from "done" to "I can see it" was private archaeology. P-7, done means verified, names the bar; this spec adds the per-feature artifact saying how a human confirms the feature.
core: Validation had no home; dogfooding spec-tictactoe proved it.
note: The spec's own #context. The design rationale lives in verify-considerations.html, a different document, and is not expected here.
visitor: The site promises work that is verifiable rather than vibe-coded. A visitor asks where the verifiable part actually lives once the build is done.

question: The copy says this runs in your favourite AI coding agent, but the install drops files into one vendor's folder. What shut every other agent out, and what shifted in the wider tooling that made supporting a second one worth doing now?
answer: `spectastic init` installs the verbs as .claude/commands/*.md, with subagents as .claude/agents/*.md — a project-local, byte-for-byte copy of the source command files — so they run only inside Claude Code and a developer working in a different agent cannot use the lifecycle at all. Cross-tool installers were always anticipated and deferred: spec 003 named a --target cursor|aider|claude|copilot|generic family and spec 031 deferred the same under TBD-cross-tool-installers. What changed is that the target became a settled standard — OpenAI's Codex converged with Claude Code and thirty-odd other tools on the Agent Skills Open Standard (.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, Dec 2025), which Codex scans from the working directory up to the repo root, and Codex's own custom-prompts path is deprecated in its favour. So the spec pulls codex forward as the first alternative host, targeting the host surface only.
core: The verbs install as Claude-Code-local command files; the Agent Skills Open Standard turned a deferred --target family into one settled format.
note: The spec's own #context. Chosen as thematically standalone: the contexts of specs 006-014 all say "today's verb is markdown and does not reach MCP", and 112-120 are one guardrail programme, so a question on either group would have ambiguous gold.
visitor: The site says "your favorite AI coding agent" and names none. This is the single most likely question from a visitor who does not use Claude Code.

question: I ran the tool's usage output and it included what looked like a tracking identifier meant for maintainers. Why would that reach the people simply running the thing?
answer: Implementation drift. The Commander .description(...) call at packages/cli/src/commands/validate.ts:20 ended in "per FR-002", and the same file's docstring at line 9 reads "Implements FR-001, FR-002, FR-014" — the LLM author appears to have carried the FR ID out of the source comment into user-facing copy. Spec FR-002, the exit-code contract, is correct as written; the leak is purely the description string. Fixed by replacing it with prose naming the exit semantics directly. Regeneration passes, because nothing in the spec or plan tells an implementer to cite FR IDs in user output.
core: Implementation drift: the FR ID was carried from the file's own docstring into the Commander description.
note: The root cause is in the card's headline and its Diagnosis. The spec's own FR-002 is explicitly not at fault, so spec.html is not expected evidence.
visitor: The site puts the validator front and centre. Odd output from the first command a visitor runs is the kind of thing they would ask about.

question: Everything in a publish ran green, and one of the pieces I pulled down afterwards was still the build from before. Why would just one of them be left stuck?
answer: Two steps in .github/workflows/publish.yml enumerate packages by name — the tag/version check and the "Move additional dist-tags" loop — and both list cli, core, schema and corpus. render is published by `pnpm publish -r`, which walks the workspace and needs no list, so it shipped on every release while remaining invisible to both checks; spec 106 had added it after the loop was written. So pre.26 published and its `next` tag moved while `latest` stayed on pre.25, and the publish job still reported success because nothing in it looks at render. Fixed by adding it to the loop and to the check beside it.
core: A dist-tag loop enumerating packages by name omitted render, which was added after the loop was written.
note: The card's headline states the root cause; its Diagnosis names the two workflow steps.
visitor: A visitor installing from a registry cares whether what they get is what was just released.

question: I accepted a proposed change, the tool said it had worked, and the next check immediately reported several problems with the document it had just written. Why would a change that succeeded leave the file broken?
answer: The author's --summary was interpolated into the changelog <span> verbatim, so element names inside that free prose became live elements in the artifact. A summary describing a change to <spec-contract> and <spec-visual> put those tags into spec.html, and four errors followed at once: an unclosed <spec-decision>, two declarations missing a required shape=, and a visual-section-gated finding reporting a Visual surface section on a spec with no user interface. The kernel builds the changelog entry by string interpolation and escapes the slug and the date but not the summary, the one field carrying free prose. Fixed by escaping it; the saving grace is that the failure was loud, so validate caught it on the next run.
core: --summary was interpolated into the changelog unescaped, so element names in it became real elements.
note: The card's headline and Diagnosis. The summary is data to display, not markup to honour.
visitor: Accepting changes is the headline workflow on the site. A visitor wants to know what happens when it goes wrong, and whether it goes wrong quietly.

question: In some generated teaching material only the final section's self-check ever did anything — answering any of the earlier ones left the page completely unresponsive. Why would just the last one work?
answer: The generated gate script declared correct, objId, checkbox and answer with `var` inside a for...of loop. `var` is function-scoped, so every change handler closed over the same bindings, and those bindings hold the final iteration's values — hence answering any quiz revealed only the last objective's answer and would tick only the last objective's checkbox. It was flagged at author time by linter S1515 and dismissed as style, and SC-003's test was structural: it asserted the script string and never executed the JS, so a broken-but-present gate passed. Fixed by block-scoping the per-iteration bindings with const, plus a test that drives a generated course in a real browser.
core: closure-over-var: per-iteration bindings declared with var inside a for...of loop.
note: The card's headline names the cause and its Diagnosis explains the scoping. The card also records that a linter flagged it and the structural test missed it.
visitor: The extended commands advertised on the site include generated explanatory material. A visitor who tried it and found it half-broken would ask exactly this.

question: I have a feature exercised from top to bottom by its harness, and the generated page that ties each requirement to the thing demonstrating it came out blank. Why would nothing be tied up?
answer: 021's test-task heuristic is path-only. TEST_PATH is /(?:(?:^|\/)tests?\/)|(?:\.(?:test|spec)\.[tj]sx?$)/ at packages/core/src/commands/verify.ts:62 and identically at packages/schema/src/rules/verify-view-stale.ts:25, so fixture-driven test tasks — paths under fixtures/, which is how every schema rule is tested — never match and the success-criterion to test join finds nothing. All three SCs therefore render "no test task cites this SC". validate stayed silent because verify-view-stale only checks consistency, empty against empty, and not completeness. The fix broadens "test task" beyond the path regex to recognise the story's Tests subsection and fixtures/ paths.
core: The test-task heuristic matched only on path, so fixture-driven tests never counted.
note: The card's headline and Diagnosis, which quote the matching rule and both call sites.
visitor: The site's claim is verifiability. A visitor whose verification page renders empty has been sold the thing that did not work.

question: The guard that is meant to stop an unfinished prototype being carried forward had been built and had a passing test, and the commands went ahead on one regardless. Why did it never take effect?
answer: An implementation gap rather than a spec gap: gateOnQuarantine shipped in packages/cli/src/state-gate.ts with a passing unit test, but it was called by no verb, so the gate function landed dead and every core verb would operate on a quarantined id. The task breakdown listed only state-gate.ts as changed and the call-site wiring into the five verb CLIs was never a task. SC-002's anti-ship guarantee still held through the validate merge gate, the primary leg; what was missing was the defence-in-depth second leg from plan D-003. Fixed by calling the gate at the top of each verb's action. Regeneration passes, because the spec and plan already mandate the refusal.
core: gateOnQuarantine was implemented and unit-tested but its call-sites were never wired, because the wiring was never a task.
note: The card's headline and Diagnosis. FR-006 in the spec is correct as written, so spec.html is not expected evidence.
visitor: The site's strongest promise is that nothing loose reaches production. A visitor would want to know about the time that promise did not hold.

question: An accessibility check was passing while one small label stayed too faint to read against what sat behind it. Why did the check not notice?
answer: The SC-003 axe sweep runs over tests/fixtures/all-components.html, and that fixture omits an unrouted <spec-triage>, so the sub-AA rule — spec-triage:not([layer]) .layer-pill in assets/spec.css — never reached the gate at all. The unrouted pill rendered salmon #e1624f on the mode surface at roughly 3:1 in light and 3.3:1 in dark, against NFR-003's requirement of 4.5:1 for every component across all four theme-by-mode combinations. The fix is a mode-aware --c-danger token, because the surface is var(--c-surface) and a single literal cannot pass both modes, plus adding the unrouted state to the fixture so the sweep covers it.
core: A coverage gap: the contrast fixture omitted an unrouted <spec-triage>, so the rule never reached the sweep.
note: The card's headline names both halves, the colour and the fixture gap; its Diagnosis names the fixture.
visitor: Every artifact on the site is read in a browser, so a visitor with an accessibility requirement asks how it is actually enforced.
